Integrated digital casting: a new method for simulating piece-mold techniques of ancient bronzes

Chinese ritual bronzes represent one of the pinnacles of technological and artistic achievement during the Shang and Zhou dynasties. The methods used to study these artifacts are of critical importance to archeological and heritage research. The traditional piece-mold casting experiment used to create these bronzes faced significant challenges, including the absence of standardization, lengthy production cycles, and great technical difficulty. This study proposes an innovative simulation method that integrates digital modeling and 3D printing to address specific challenges in traditional piece-mold casting experiments. Using a Shang dynasty Ding (tripod pot) as a case study, the approach employs digital modeling and substitute materials to standardize mold design, enhance precision, and reduce production time from several weeks to under 40 h. Preserving technological features such as casting joints and mold marks, the method provides a reproducible heuristic framework for exploring hypotheses about ancient sectional mold design, craft education, and technical validation.

Chinese ritual bronzes embody both early technological achievements and artistic refinement within Chinese civilization. As tangible heritage, they provide irreplaceable material evidence for studying the ritual systems, metallurgy, and artistic evolution of the Shang dynasty (ca. 1600–1046 B.C.) and Zhou dynasty (1046–256 B.C.); as intangible cultural heritage, piece mold casting technique served as a crucial foundation for bronze ritual vessel production in China during the Bronze Age1, reflecting the technical philosophy of ancient artisans. In contrast to the lost-wax process––widely used in ancient Mediterranean and Mesopotamian civilizations to cast objects integrally from a single wax model––the early Chinese bronze casting technique began with the creation of a model2. The ceramic piece-mold casting technology is a unique feature of ancient Chinese bronze production3, which involved applying clay around a model to form the outer mold, which was then divided into sections to allow for its removal. Simultaneously, a clay core, or “inner mold” was prepared. The outer mold and core were assembled together, with the gap between them forming the mold cavity that defined the vessel’s thickness4. Finally, molten alloy was poured into this space; after cooling, the outer mold and core were removed to reveal the bronze object5. Bronzes were the material reflection of core cultural ideas6. Therefore, a comprehensive investigation into this distinctive piece-mold casting technology is crucial for deciphering the technical sophistication, cultural values, and developmental trajectory of early Chinese metallurgy.

Molds are amongst the most important elements of Bronze Age technology7. The essence of the bronze piece-mold casting technique lies in its sectional mold design. This process involves dividing the three-dimensional form of the vessel in order to fabricate separate outer mold sections and a core, which are then assembled to form a complete mold design–– including the core and the resulting casting cavity. The layout of parting surfaces is guided by the geometry of the vessel to ensure dimensional conformity. For example, a bronze Ding (tripod pot) inculding legs, body and handles are illustrated in Fig. 1. The success of a casting largely depends on its sectional mold design. To advance the understanding and reconstruction of this technique, several research approaches have been established in academia. These primarily include the systematic examination of extant bronzes, the analysis of excavated molds and models, and experimental archeology.
Schematic diagram of sectional mold design (using a Shang Dynasty Ding as an Example).

Careful examination of the artifacts has always been the first step in studying ancient Chinese bronzes8. Systematic examination of bronze surfaces allows researchers to infer the original sectional mold design from the casting seams, which were formed during mold assembly and subsequent casting. This approach is exemplified by studies that have reconstructed the mold configuration of a double-ram Zun (wine vessel) based on surface marks9, and identified a three-part structure in an Eastern Zhou Ding (tripod pot) through analysis of its body joints10. However, this method is inherently subjective, as casting joints are often difficult to detect–– either obscured by tightly fitted mold sections or removed during the post-casting finishing process11.

The analysis of excavated molds, models, and cores offers more direct evidence for understanding sectional mold design. For instance, the clay molds, models, and cores from the site offer tangible material for such research12. Furthermore, the correlation of excavated molds with corresponding bronze objects has enabled the reconstruction of casting processes for specific vessel types13. Nonetheless, complete clay molds remain rare and have only been found at a limited number of casting sites.

While the above methods focus on isolated stages of the casting process, a holistic perspective requires the integrated approach offered by experimental archeology. Building on the methods already mentioned, experimental archeology reconstructs procedures such as mold-making and pouring to study ancient techniques14. Through experimental reconstruction of casting processes, researchers can reproduce bronze production and test hypothesized sectional mold designs against archeologically observed features. Representative studies include the successful replication of a Shang dynasty bronze Gu (wine vessel) using a two-part sectional mold and core15, as well as the recreation of the linked-casting technique of an Eastern Zhou bronze horse bit16. Such reconstructions provide direct and tangible verification of ancient craftsmanship and sectional mold design. Experimental archeology focusing on bronze casting not only deepens scholarly understanding of ancient manufacturing techniques but also contributes to the scientific preservation and transmission of this intangible cultural heritage.

Despite its advantages, the broader application of traditional piece-mold casting experiments faces significant challenges. More than forty distinct vessel types from the Shang and Zhou periods have been documented17, systematic experimental research in studies-led studies by archaeologists remains limited to a few representative forms––such as the Ding, Gui, Zun, and Gu––due to high experimental barriers, and the issues addressed are often generic and narrow in scope18.

Even when a vessel is successfully replicated, it is difficult to confirm whether the result accurately reflects ancient practice, as multiple plausible sectioning strategies could have been employed. Consequently, experimental outcomes are often suggestive rather than conclusive. The same limitation applies to any replication method, including the one proposed here. However, this highlights the need for complementary tools that can systematically compare multiple design hypotheses under controlled conditions—not to resolve the ambiguity definitively, but to identify which hypotheses are geometrically feasible and consistent with archeological observations before committing to time-intensive traditional experiments. Traditional piece-mold casting experiments thus face three major challenges: the absence of standardization, lengthy production cycles, and great technical difficulty, which together contribute to persistent research gaps.

First, the absence of standardization is evident in the lack of unified technical specifications, often leading to dimensional inconsistencies in final castings. The demanding procedures—such as forming molds in a single session and carving their surfaces rapidly yet meticulously—make consistent alignment difficult to achieve. Minor operational errors frequently introduce defects, requiring extensive post-casting finishing19. Moreover, outcomes remain heavily reliant on the artisan’s individual skill, even when material compositions and operating temperatures are kept consistent.

Second, lengthy production cycles result from the inherently inefficient iteration of sectional mold designs. Each stage—from model and mold creation through drying, firing, and pouring—requires laborious manual trial-and-error adjustments. The air-drying phase for clay molds is particularly time-consuming, often extending the total production cycle to approximately 50 days20. This protracted timeline severely limits the number of design iterations that can be realistically tested in a research project, hindering systematic comparison of alternative sectioning hypotheses.

Third, great technical difficulty impedes wider adoption of the process. The process demands substantial labor and material resources, along with extreme technical conditions such as mold firing at temperatures up to 1100 °C and precise control over pouring temperature and speed21. Combined with a strong dependence on artisan experience, this results in low standardization and poor reproducibility.

In recent years, 3D printing technology has introduced new possibilities for cultural heritage preservation and craft reproduction. This flexible technology provides the advantages of customization, prototyping, various fabrication techniques, and complex geometries at a low cost in a short timeframe22, and has been widely applied in artifact restoration and conservation23.

Building on this potential, this study develops an integrated digital casting approach, which extends 3D printing technology to piece-mold casting simulation through material substitution and process digitization. This method uses low-density gypsum and low-melting-point alloys as research proxies (not as claims about ancient materials), while systematically modeling mold sectional design through parametric methods. By establishing precise control over material properties, printing parameters, and dimensional accuracy, the method enables researchers to isolate and examine the geometric variables of sectional mold design, reducing the influence of artisan skill variability and high-temperature constraints during the hypothesis-testing phase. Furthermore, it allows for faster iteration of mold designs while preserving all essential craft characteristics, such as casting joints and mold marks. This method is intended as a supplementary tool for hypothesis generation and pre-testing, not as a replacement for traditional clay-based experiments or as evidence of ancient practices. It may also facilitate public education and heritage transmission by lowering barriers to hands-on understanding of piece-mold logic.

This study utilized Blender, a free and open-source 3D creation suite that supports various modes, including polygonal modeling, curve modeling, sculpting, and precision modeling. It offers a suite of industrial-grade tools capable of generating and exporting high-quality, 3D-printable models.

The Boolean operations functionality in Blender provided the mathematical tools essential for the sectional mold design in this study. Based on the modeled Shang dynasty ding, the Difference Boolean operation was used to perform geometric subtraction between the ding and pre-defined fan-shaped sectional volumes, precisely generating the digital parting surfaces for the outer mold sections and the core. Furthermore, interlocking alignment, such as tenon-and-mortise features, is essential for standardizing sectional design; the Union Boolean operation was employed to integrate alignment structures on the parting surfaces.

The 3D printing was performed on a Bambu Lab A1 printer, which employs the FDM technique— a process that creates 3D structures through the layer-by-layer melt-extrusion of a plastic filament24. For the printing material, PLA (polylactic acid) was chosen as the primary material. PLA is a biodegradable, easily compostable, and non-toxic material obtained from renewable resources such as sugar beets and corn25, and it also possesses good mechanical processing performance with low shrinkage26. These characteristics collectively support the goal of achieving higher surface quality in the printed objects27.

To acquire first-hand, detailed insights and establish a procedural workflow of traditional piece-mold casting techniques, simulated reconstruction experiments were conducted at a renowned workshop specializing in this craft (Xianyang Bronze Piece-Mold Casting Research Institute). An early Shang dynasty Ding was selected as the research object. The complete bronze casting process was documented through direct observation, which was then summarized into a technical workflow (Fig. 2).
The piece-mold casting process for bronze vessels.
The execution of the piece-mold casting experiment faces four major practical challenges:
The creation of the model demands great skill in carving, while the formation of the molds requires proficient operational experience.

Since most stages of the process are based on the craftsman’s experience, consistent, quantifiable parameters are often lacking, e.g., the composition of the mold clay, thickness of the clay flakes, air-drying time, and firing temperature. Furthermore, parameters such as drying times for molds cannot be precisely predetermined, as they vary with geographical location and environmental conditions due to factors like ambient temperature and humidity.
Despite the short pouring stage, multiple points in the process are prone to failure; any failure necessitates restarting the entire procedure from the beginning.
The entire production cycle is protracted, typically requiring approximately one to two months.

In summary, traditional piece-mold casting experiments face significant constraints: their reliance on artisan expertise, lack of standardized workflow, a lengthy production cycle, a high risk of failure, and substantial investment in both labor and material costs. These limitations hinder both the broader application of the craft in research and the development of accessible, time-efficient workflows for modern cultural heritage education. Consequently, optimizing the technical process through technological means and establishing a more systematic and reproducible workflow can be valuable for research purposes and for lowering barriers to educational engagement with this craft.

To address the inherent challenges in traditional piece-mold casting experiments–– such as the lack of standardization, extended process cycles, and high technical requirements–– and to explore scientific rationale and transferability of section mold design in a more systematic manner, this study proposes an integrated digital casting methodology. This optimized workflow is centered on the digital reconstruction of sectional logic using 3D printing technology(Fig. 3).
Optimized workflow for piece-mold casting experiment.

The scheme introduces innovations primarily through digital sectional modeling and material substitution. The process is as follows: First, a 3D model of a Shang dynasty Ding is created in Blender software. Through Boolean operations, the vessel’s geometry is decomposed into fan-shaped outer mold sections and a core, effectively achieving “digital mold replication”. Subsequently, the negative (cavity) part of these outer molds and the core are generated using the same Boolean tools. Next, the mold negatives are fabricated via a 3D printer with PLA filament to ensure the geometric accuracy of the parting surfaces. A low-density gypsum slurry is then poured into these printed mold negatives to create gypsum molds, simulating the physical characteristics of traditional clay molds. Finally, a low-melting-point alloy is used instead of high-temperature alloy liquid for the pouring stage, thus eliminating the high-temperature process.

Integrated digital casting preserves characteristic craft features on the final cast object, such as casting joints and mold marks, while reducing the design validation cycle from the traditional 1–2 months to just 40 h. It thus reduces the traditional process’s dependence on artisan experience and specific environmental conditions for the purpose of hypothesis testing, offering a more systematic and reproducible way to explore the core logic of sectional mold design and casting principles in research and educational contexts.
3D modeling based on reconstructed sectional mold design logic

In traditional piece-mold casting, the mold for a simple round vessel was typically divided into three identical sections28, a practice that often produces sharp-angled geometric structures. These sharp angles can lead to stress concentration during mold assembly, causing corner breakage or misalignment of the mold sections. To address this issue, this study proposes a modified cylindrical sectional geometry for the molds. The original flat joining surfaces on the exterior of the outer molds (see Figs. 1 and 2) were redesigned as curved surfaces. This modification can help achieve a more even distribution of forces during mold assembly and the subsequent embedding process. Due to traditional fabrication constraints, three-part molds typically form sharp corners and lack smooth transitions at the joints, making them vulnerable to damage and displacement during handling.

In contrast to the traditional design, the modified outer mold for the Ding consists of three 120-degree fan-shaped cylindrical segments (Fig. 4C-(d)). The arcuate parting surfaces of these segments conform naturally to the curved profile of Ding’s body, distribute pressure evenly upon assembly, and utilize self-aligning characteristics to minimize manual adjustment. Furthermore, Boolean operations enables the creation of well-fitting mold assemblies. By integrating interlocking tenon-and-mortise features, precise positioning of the mold sections is facilitated during assembly, thereby reducing deviations inherent in the traditional process and significantly enhancing assembly accuracy. Based on this modeling logic, digital models for casting both the outer molds and the core were created, corresponding to Fig. 4A-(d) and Fig. 4B-(d), respectively. The final assembly of the core and outer molds is presented in Fig. 4C-(c) and (d).
A Making the Molds; B Making the Core; C Assembling; D The modeling process of mold negatives; E The modeling process of core negatives.

Building upon the digital models of the outer molds and core for the Ding, a set of production negatives––or “mold of mold”––was designed for casting these components. Continuing the same digital sectioning methodology and workflow, Boolean operations were employed: the volume of the outer mold section was subtracted from a fan-shaped cylindrical base, which was then appropriately segmented. Concurrently, the Union Boolean operation was used to integrate interlocking tenon-and-mortise features, ensuring precise position and stability of the mold negatives during assembly. The disassembled negatives for the outer mold are shown in Fig. 4D-(e), and their assembled state in Fig. 4D-(c). Similarly, the disassembled negatives for the core are shown in Fig. 4E-(e), with the assembled version presented in Fig. 4E-(f).
After completing the Blender model of Ding’s mold negatives, each design was exported as an STL file and imported into Bambu Studio, the slicing software for the Bambu Lab A1 printer.

FDM can replicate fine details of artifacts with high accuracy and at relatively low cost, enabling millimeter-level repairs and producing consistent mold forms29; however, the surface roughness of FDM parts is deeply affected by the layer height of the prototypes30. Therefore, in selecting the print parameters to balance high surface quality with reasonable speed, it is essential to consider that all of these parameters influence the quality and properties of the printed parts31. The printer’s standard 0.4 mm nozzle was used with a layer height of 0.1 mm. This configuration achieves stable surface quality while maintaining a reasonably fast print time. The “Normal” support structure type was used for the prints. The top and bottom Z-distances for the supports were set to 0.2 mm to facilitate their later removal. All other parameters were maintained at their default settings.

One of the core advantages of 3D printing is its ability to transcend geometric constraints, enabling the fabrication of complex forms such as multi-curved surfaces, structures that are particularly suitable for the accurate restoration and innovative reinterpretation of cultural artifacts32. For geometries with overhangs, support structures are necessary, but their contact points with the model surface can leave residue upon removal, which may affect the precision of the mold negatives. To minimize such issues, the print preview function was used to evaluate support quantity, contact area, and printing time. Based on this evaluation, a printing strategy was chosen to reduce both the number of supports and their impact on functional surfaces, as outlined in Table 1.

Among the options, Strategy 1 requires no support and represents the ideal case. Strategy 2 generates supports that avoid contact with critical functional surfaces. Strategy 3 utilizes the least support material and achieves the smallest contact area with the model. The selected strategies thus achieve good surface quality while conserving material and providing a practical print speed. The final printed models are shown in Fig. 5.

a 3D-printed outer mold negatives; b Assembled configuration of the outer mold negatives; c 3D-printed core negatives; d Assembled configuration of the core negatives.

In bronze casting, the surface of the final object is determined by the quality of the mold33. For the purpose of rapidly producing molds that capture geometric detail, this study uses low-density gypsum, which is primarily composed of calcium sulfate hemihydrate (CaSO₄•0.5H₂O), as a substitute for traditional clay in mold making. The use of low-melting-point alloy is advantageous due to its compatibility with gypsum molds, which are easier to form and yield consistent surface quality. When combined with 3D-printed negatives, this approach allows for relatively rapid production of gypsum molds suitable for hypothesis testing.

The quality of the gypsum molds can be governed by the water-to-powder ratio of the slurry. The ratio directly determines the material’s porosity, hardness, and surface roughness. A higher water content improves slurry fluidity but results in a more porous and weaker structure after curing. While increased porosity can be beneficial for venting gases during metal pouring, it significantly reduces mechanical strength. Conversely, reducing the water content increases density and hardness but may lead to incomplete filling of the mold negatives due to poor slurry flow, resulting in voids and other defects.

To evaluate the effects of different ratios, a standardized procedure was followed: a layer of petroleum jelly was applied to the contact surfaces of the 3D-printed mold negatives. Six batches of gypsum slurry with different water-to-powder ratios ranging from 0.75:1 to 2:1 were prepared and poured into the molds. After setting, the gypsum molds were dried at 50 °C to stabilize their form and remove residual moisture, and the parting lines were smoothed. By systematically examining the molds, the influence of the mix ratio on surface quality and structural integrity was assessed.

The mold assembly for the simulated casting of the Ding consists of three outer mold sections and a core. After assembling the gypsum mold sections at the predetermined angles, rubber bands were used for alignment and to secure the assembly. To address potential gaps at the mold joints, gypsum slurry with a 1:1 water-to-powder ratio was applied as a sealant. Once the filler had solidified to form a complete casting cavity, the mold assembly was buried in a container of sand. The surrounding sand was compacted firmly, leaving only the pouring gate exposed to prevent leakage of the molten alloy.

For the casting, a low-melting-point alloy was employed. The alloy is composed of 50% bismuth, 12.5% tin, 12.5% cadmium, and 25% lead, with a melting point of 70 degrees. The process involved pouring, followed by cooling, demolding, and surface cleaning. The resulting casting was then inspected under magnification, with a focus on the rim, body, and legs, to evaluate the sharpness, wall thickness uniformity, and the presence of any surface defects.
Molding effectiveness of the Gypsum molds

The introduction of low-density gypsum powder to simulate clay molds represents a useful methodological approach in this study. While gypsum differs from traditional clay in material composition, its dimensional stability and rapid setting time make it particularly suitable for replicating the geometric logic of sectional mold design, in the context of hypothesis testing, allowing researchers to focus on form and assembly rather than material behavior. Traditional clay molds require a lengthy and complex sequence of processes—including model making, clay tamping, pattern carving, air-drying, and firing. This approach demands considerable experience, has a long production cycle, and often results in a high failure rate. In contrast, creating molds from low-density gypsum involves only mixing the powder with water in a specific ratio, pouring the slurry into a mold negative, demolding after setting, and then drying. For the purpose of quickly producing molds that capture geometric detail, this liquid formation method is relatively simpler and offers practical control.

The characteristically porous structure of gypsum effectively vents gases from the mold cavity during metal pouring, helping to prevent casting defects, while simultaneously achieving a level of detail reproduction comparable to that of clay molds. Importantly, the physical properties of gypsum allow the finished mold to be cleanly separated from the casting through simple tapping, notably reducing both procedural complexity and time. This single-use characteristic preserves the essential traditional logic of “One mold for one vessel” inherent to piece-mold technology, while also enabling production in controlled settings such as educational workshops.

After the gypsum molds had been fully dried (see Fig. 6 for the production process), comprehensive testing was conducted on molds of different mixing ratios. Surface quality was evaluated by inspecting key areas such as the rim, main body structure, and legs. Molds with a water-to-powder ratio of 1:0.75 and 1:1 exhibited good surface quality, with sharp cavity contours that generally met the requirements for adequate casting and demonstrated good detail reproduction compared to other formulas. Samples of other ratios, while capable of forming the basic shape, showed particle agglomeration and localized micro-cracks under 50x magnification and were therefore excluded from further consideration.
Fig. 6: Fabrication process of the Gypsum molds.
a Pouring the gypsum slurry; b, c, d Removing the outer mold negatives; e Removing the core negatives.

As determined by mercury intrusion porosimetry, pore structure parameters of gypsum molds with different formulations were analyzed. Although the 1:0.75 ratio mold delivered good detail fidelity, its low porosity caused difficulties in demolding, where the dense structure risked damaging the precision casting during removal. In contrast, the 1:1 formulation provided moderate porosity and, upon hardening, formed a dense and robust solid skeleton with a fine, uniform pore structure. This resulted in a gypsum block that combined adequate mechanical strength with a smooth surface finish while accurately reproducing the cavity geometry. By effectively balancing molding quality and process safety, the 1:1 ratio was thus identified as a suitable choice for gypsum molds.

By employing a low-melting-point alloy for casting, the metal is allowed to remain sufficiently fluid at low temperatures, ensuring it completely fills the intricate cavity of the gypsum mold. As a result, the cast piece exhibits sharp pattern edges and uniform wall thickness. By eliminating the hazards and specialized equipment required for traditional high-temperature alloy pouring, the low-temperature operation enhances safety and reduces the necessary skill level for this specific alloy and mold combination. Furthermore, the alloy’s recyclability may be useful for repeated testing in research or educational contexts.

The Ding was cast using a 1:1 ratio of gypsum mold and a low-melting-point alloy. The alloy, with a melting point of 70 °C, was poured at 80 °C. The casting process is illustrated in Fig. 7. The molten metal successfully filled the fine cavity details, producing a casting that closely reproduced the intended surface patterns. This outcome demonstrates the high degree of detail fidelity achievable with this approach. Compared to the stringent requirements of traditional high-temperature pouring, this method can provide the piece-mold casting experience to be safely and practically applied in educational or research settings.

Casting practice based on a Shang Bronzeware
To validate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology in replicating characteristic features of cultural artifacts, a Ding was cast based on a Shang dynasty taotie-patterned Ding.

Building on the established experimental framework, a 3D modle of a taotie-patterned Ding was created. Using Boolean operations, the corresponding outer mold sections and core were digitally generated. These components were then 3D-printed as mold negatives, adhering to the previously determined optimal parameters and material. Limited by the printer’s build volume, the resulting outer mold negatives were 23 cm in height. A gypsum slurry with the optimal 1:1 mix ratio was poured into these printed negatives; after drying and setting, the gypsum outer molds and core were obtained.

The gypsum mold assembly was then secured, and gaps at the joints were sealed using the same 1:1 gypsum slurry. Once fully dry, the entire assembly was buried in a container of sand for alloy casting. After complete cooling, the outer gypsum molds were broken away, and the core was removed. Excess material, including the pouring gate, was then cleaned from the surface to reveal the final cast taotie-patterned Ding. The complete fabrication process is documented in Fig. 8.
Fig. 8: Fabrication process of the taotie-patterned Ding.

a Modeling the taotie-patterned Ding; b Modeling the outer mold and core for the taotie-patterned Ding; c 3D printing the mold negatives for the Ding; d Assembling the mold negatives; e Gypsum outer mold for the taotie-patterned Ding; f Assembling the gypsum mold for the Ding; g Breaking the mold after pouring; h Finished casting.

To evaluate the experimental casting outcome, a comparative analysis was conducted among three objects: a Shang dynasty taotie-patterned Ding, a Ding made by traditional methods (whose production process is shown in Fig. 2), and the Ding produced using the integrated digital casting method. The comparison focused on key piece-mold casting features—including patterns, mold marks, rim—to examine specific technical details. The results of this analysis are summarized in Table 2.
Table 2 Comparison of the craftsmanship details of the taotie-patterned Ding
The comparative analysis suggested differences between the traditional experiment and integrated digital casting across four key technical aspects:

Wall thickness control: The traditional method relies on manually rolling clay flakes, which offers limited precision over thickness uniformity. In contrast, integrated digital casting employs parametric modeling and high-precision gypsum molds to produce a Ding with improved wall thickness uniformity and a consistently thinner profile, achieved through precise mathematical control.

Pattern reproduction fidelity: The traditional process requires patterns to be manually carved onto the outer mold surface. Their depth and proportions depend on the artisan’s experience, often leading to uneven relief height and variations in line width. Integrated digital casting directly replicates the digital model of the original patterns via 3D-printed mold negatives, ensuring consistent pattern depth and accurate proportions for a complete and faithful representation of details.

Mold marks and assembly precision: While the traditional process often leads to prominent and irregular mold joins due to manual assembly misalignment—requiring extensive post-casting finishing—integrated digital casting achieves a critical balance. By incorporating integrated alignment features and standardized sectional mold design, it significantly improves assembly accuracy while still preserving intentionally designed mold marks as authentic process signatures. These retained features demonstrate replication of the sectional mold structure successfully, with consistently narrower widths and higher dimensional control than traditional methods. Furthermore, in terms of surface roughness, castings produced by this method achieved roughness levels comparable to those made with refined clay in traditional piece-mold casting, with the added benefit of greater uniformity.

Rim formation: In contrast to the traditional method, which often results in uneven thickness or subtle deformation along the rim due to manual mold assembly and clay shifting, the integrated digital casting approach achieves markedly improved rim regularity and structural integrity, well-defined rim contour, closely matching the morphological features observed on original artifacts.

Most notably, integrated digital casting in our experimental setup achieves a reduction in production time. The traditional process requires a minimum of 50 days to fabricate a single mold set, even for a skilled artisan. In contrast, integrated digital casting completes the entire cycle in under 40 h. By integrating rapid iteration via 3D-printed negatives and low-temperature casting, the process can be operated by one person for this specific workflow. This significant reduction in time and labor may facilitate repeated hypothesis testing and educational engagement, as summarized in Table 3.
Table 3 Comparison of the core advantages of 3D printing and material innovation in bronze piece mold casting

Characteristic features of Shang and Zhou bronze piece-mold casting are often identified by examining mold marks on object surfaces and analyzing excavated mold fragments. This evidence supports plausible hypotheses about sectional design. However, simulation experiments—essential to this line of inquiry—face three persistent challenges: a lack of standardization, lengthy process cycles, and high technical barriers, all of which affect both educational applications and scholarly advancement.

As a potential response to these limitations, this study introduces an integrated digital casting method that combines 3D printing and alternative materials within the traditional experimental framework. As the build volume of mainstream 3D printing systems encompasses the typical dimensions of Shang and Zhou dynasty bronze artifacts (ranging from several centimeters to around 2 meters), this approach is broadly applicable in terms of object scale. Using Boolean operations, 3D-printed mold negatives are generated that conform precisely to the vessel’s geometry while adhering to traditional molding principles. Selected printing parameters can help minimize support structures and production time, while an ideal gypsum mix ratio, determined through microscopic analysis, enhances mold quality. The process concludes with pouring a low-melting-point alloy, yielding castings that preserve characteristic piece-mold features.

This integrated approach maintains the core sectional logic while modifying its execution through precision 3D printing, gypsum mold formation, and low-temperature alloy pouring. It offers a way to establish quantifiable parameters, reduces production time from weeks to approximately 40 h, and reduces dependence on specialized craftsmanship and high-temperature operations for the purpose of hypothesis testing. The resulting framework enables more accessible, efficient simulation of ancient casting technology under controlled laboratory conditions.

Consequently, this method is efficient, reproducible, and cost-effective, making it potentially suitable for public education and heritage transmission. While it does not replicate the full high-temperature casting process, the resulting objects retain essential craft characteristics and adhere to core principles such as sectional design, mold assembly logic, and the “One mold for one vessel” concept. It offers a way to reimagine piece-mold casting for research and educational purposes, providing a more quantifiable and replicable technical pathway without claiming to replace traditional craft knowledge. While it does not replicate the full material complexity of ancient casting, it provides a practical means for validating sectional design hypotheses and enables the expanded reconstruction of various vessel types. Through parametric modeling and standardized procedures, this study offers repeatable and efficient technical support for related work, contributing to the study and educational outreach of piece-mold casting as intangible cultural heritage.
